question.text:
A patient arrives at the emergency department with a fractured humeral shaft, exhibiting wrist drop and inability to extend their fingers and thumb. Among the following motor functions, which would you expect to be the last to return to normal?
Answer Choices: (A) Adduction of the thumb (B) Wrist extension in radial deviation (C) Flexion of the index finger DIP joint (D) Supination of the forearm (E) Extension of the middle finger MCP joint (F) Index finger MCP hyperextension (G) Abduction of the thumb (H) Thumb MCP hyperextension (I) Middle finger MCP extension (J) Full extension of the elbow

options.C: Flexion of the index finger DIP joint
options.E: Extension of the middle finger MCP joint

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The patient presents with wrist drop and inability to extend fingers and thumb, indicating a disruption of the radial nerve or its branches. The radial nerve innervates the muscles responsible for wrist extension, finger extension, and thumb abduction and extension. The order of recovery of these functions follows the path of the nerve. Thumb MCP hyperextension is the last function to recover because it is innervated by the posterior interosseous nerve (PIN), which is a branch of the radial nerve and is the most distal branch. The other options are innervated by the median nerve, which is more proximal and recovers earlier.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: The patient's inability to extend the fingers and thumb, along with wrist drop, strongly suggests radial nerve involvement.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While other nerve injuries could cause some of these deficits, the combination of wrist drop and inability to extend the fingers and thumb points most strongly to radial nerve damage. Median nerve injury would primarily affect thumb abduction and opposition, and wrist flexion, and ulnar nerve injury would affect the little finger and ring finger.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient has a fractured humeral shaft with wrist drop and finger extension inability. The humerus fracture likely affects the ulnar nerve, which innervates the intrinsic muscles of the hand. Intrinsic muscles control thumb and finger movements. Hyperextension of the index finger MCP joint (F) involves the extensor digitorum communis muscle, which is innervated by the radial nerve. Radial nerve injury would typically cause wrist drop and finger extension weakness. Since the radial nerve recovers last after a fracture, this function would be the last to return to normal.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: Wrist drop and finger extension inability
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: Radiculopathy, tendon rupture, or nerve compression were considered but ruled out due to the specific clinical presentation matching a humeral shaft fracture with associated nerve injury.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient presents with a fractured humeral shaft and wrist drop with inability to extend fingers and thumb, indicating injury to the radial nerve. The radial nerve innervates extensors of the wrist and fingers, with motor fibers to wrist extensors (radial deviation) being among the last to recover due to their dependence on the most distal nerve fibers. Motor recovery follows a proximal-to-distal pattern, and wrist extension in radial deviation is typically the last to return.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: Wrist drop and inability to extend fingers and thumb are classic signs of radial nerve injury, and wrist extension in radial deviation is innervated by the most distal branches of the radial nerve, making it the last to recover.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Other nerve injuries (e.g., median, ulnar) were considered but ruled out because the clinical presentation is specific to radial nerve dysfunction, which is the most common injury associated with humeral shaft fractures.
